sections.markdown:
## C2 — Confusable pairs and knowledge-graph hints: stop versus yield, regulatory versus guide signs, road marker numbers, center line passing rules and where to stop
Confusable pairs among regulatory, guide and route signs, center line and lane markings, and the stopping points at stop lines and crosswalks, followed by continuation facts; each block ties to one handbook page, and hint metadata sits only in the trailing line of a block.

FACT_ID: sec08-R01 | anchor: A01
Regulatory signs in general state laws you must follow, while the version with a red circle and slash specifically forbids whatever action is pictured beneath it. [A01]
Why it matters: group regulatory signs; confusable rule sign versus prohibition sign.
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0067]

FACT_ID: sec08-R02 | anchor: A02
The stop sign is a red octagon with white letters, while the yield sign is a downward-pointing red and white triangle whose letters are red. [A02]
Why it matters: group regulatory signs; confusable stop versus yield shape.
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0068]

FACT_ID: sec08-R03 | anchor: A02
A stop sign requires a stop and then yielding, whereas a yield sign requires slowing and letting right-of-way traffic cross before you enter. [A02]
Why it matters: group regulatory signs; confusable stop versus yield action.
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0068]

FACT_ID: sec08-R04 | anchor: A02
Speed limit signs set a maximum that applies in ideal conditions, so they are not a guarantee that the posted speed is safe at every moment. [A02]
Why it matters: group regulatory signs; difficulty medium.
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0068]

FACT_ID: sec08-R05 | anchor: A03
Guide signs, in green, brown or blue, give information and directions rather than stating laws to obey. [A03]
Why it matters: group guide signs; confusable guide versus regulatory.
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0069]

FACT_ID: sec08-R06 | anchor: A03
On the S road marker the county number comes first and the road number comes last, and each county keeps its own separate set of secondary road numbers. [A03]
Why it matters: group route signs; confusable county number versus road number.
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0069]

FACT_ID: sec08-R07 | anchor: A04
In rural areas secondary system roads are not designed as through routes, which is why drivers who do not know the area should not normally use them. [A04]
Why it matters: group route signs; difficulty low.
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0070]

FACT_ID: sec08-R08 | anchor: A05
On a two-direction roadway, one yellow marking pattern allows passing only for the driver who has the dashed line on their side. [A05]
Why it matters: group pavement markings; confusable dashed side versus solid side.
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0071]

FACT_ID: sec08-R09 | anchor: A07
When a stop line and a crosswalk are both present and the stop line comes first, you stop at the stop line rather than at the crosswalk. [A07]
Why it matters: group stopping points; confusable stop line versus crosswalk.
Source: [A07 -> pdf-0073]

FACT_ID: sec08-R10 | anchor: A07
With no stop line and no crosswalk, the stopping point is the spot nearest the intersection where you can see both ways without moving into cross traffic. [A07]
Why it matters: group stopping points; difficulty medium.
Source: [A07 -> pdf-0073]
